title: Well-definedness of the Euler characteristic
statement:
Let $k$ be a field, let $X$ be a scheme proper over $k$ [def-weil-proper-morphism] and let $\mathcal F$ be a coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module [pqf-def-coherent]. Each cohomology group $H^i(X,\mathcal F)$ [pqf-def-cohomology] ($i\geq0$) is a $\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)$-module, hence a $k$-vector space through the structure map $k\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)$. Then every $H^i(X,\mathcal F)$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, and the set $\{i\geq0: H^i(X,\mathcal F)\neq0\}$ is finite. Hence
$$
\chi(X,\mathcal F)=\sum_{i\geq0}(-1)^i\dim_kH^i(X,\mathcal F)
$$
[def-weil-vector-space-dimension] is a finite sum of integers, a well-defined element of $\mathbf Z$.

proof.text: *Setup.* Let $f:X\to S:=\operatorname{Spec}k$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] be the structure morphism. By [def-weil-proper-morphism] $f$ is proper, i.e. separated, of finite type and universally closed; being of finite type it is locally of finite type and quasi-compact [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. The base $S=\operatorname{Spec}k$ is affine and has one point, so it is quasi-compact; the ring $k$ is Noetherian (its only ideals are $0$ and $k$), so $S$ is locally Noetherian [pqf-def-locnoeth] (the cover by $S$ itself).

source.place: Definition 0BEJ (varieties-definition-euler-characteristic) and the paragraph after it: 'Let $k$ be a field. Let $X$ be a proper scheme over $k$'

proof.text: *$\mathcal F$ is quasi-coherent.* Since $S$ is locally Noetherian and $f$ is locally of finite type, $X$ is locally Noetherian [pqf-lem-locnoeth-lft]. On a locally Noetherian scheme a coherent module is quasi-coherent (of finite type) [pqf-lem-coherent-ft-locnoeth]; so $\mathcal F$ is quasi-coherent.

*Finite dimensionality.* Apply [lem-pc-coherent-hi] to the proper morphism $f:X\to S$ with $S=\operatorname{Spec}(A)$, $A=k$ Noetherian (Step 1), and the coherent module $\mathcal F$: each $H^i(X,\mathcal F)$ is a finite $k$-module, the $k$-module structure being the one through $f^\sharp:k=\Gamma(S,\mathcal O_S)\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)$, i.e. the structure map of the statement. A finitely generated $k$-vector space is finite-dimensional: a finite generating family contains a basis, so $\dim_kH^i(X,\mathcal F)\in\mathbf Z_{\geq0}$ is defined [def-weil-vector-space-dimension].

source.place: Lemma 02O6 (coherent-lemma-proper-over-affine-cohomology-finite), cited in varieties.tex after Definition 0BEJ: 'each of these spaces is finite dimensional'

proof.text: *Vanishing in large degrees.* Since $S$ is quasi-compact (Step 1), [lem-pc-coherent-hi] gives an integer $n\geq0$ with $R^if_*\mathcal F=0$ for all $i\geq n$. The morphism $f$ is quasi-compact and separated with $S$ affine, and $\mathcal F$ is quasi-coherent (Step 2), so [lem-pc-cohomology-sections-affine-base] gives isomorphisms $H^i(X,\mathcal F)\cong\Gamma(S,R^if_*\mathcal F)$; for $i\geq n$ the right side is $\Gamma(S,0)=0$. Hence $\{i\geq0:H^i(X,\mathcal F)\neq0\}\subseteq\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ is finite.

source.place: paragraph after Definition 0BEJ: 'only a finite number of the vector spaces $H^i(X,\mathcal{F})$ are nonzero (Cohomology of Schemes, Lemma 01XJ)'; the passage from $R^if_*$ to $H^i$ is Lemma 01XK

proof.text: *Conclusion.* By Steps 3 and 4 the family $\bigl((-1)^i\dim_kH^i(X,\mathcal F)\bigr)_{i\geq0}$ consists of integers [def-weil-vector-space-dimension] and vanishes for $i\geq n$ (a zero vector space has dimension $0$), so $\chi(X,\mathcal F)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(-1)^i\dim_kH^i(X,\mathcal F)\in\mathbf Z$ is a finite sum, independent of the choice of $n$ (the added terms are $0$).

source.place: paragraph after Definition 0BEJ: 'Thus $\chi(X, \mathcal{F}) \in \mathbf{Z}$ is well defined.'
